title: Features
jupyter: python3
---

**Skimpy** provides:

- a way to create summary statistics of **pandas** or **Polars** dataframes, using the `skim()` function, and print them to your console via the [rich](https://github.com/willmcgugan/rich) package
- support for summarising boolean, numeric, datetime, date, timedelta, string, and category datatypes
- a command line interface to `skim` CSV, parquet, and SQLite files
- intelligent rounding of numerical values to 4 significant figures
- a way to export the visual summary statistics to lossless formats namely SVG or HTML, or to plain text
- a way to further work with the summary statistics, by returning them as a dictionary
- a way to clean up messy column names in both **pandas** and **Polars** dataframes

When using **skimpy**, please be aware that *numerical columns are rounded to 4 significant figures*. You should also be aware that *any timezone-aware datetimes are converted into their naive equivalents*.

You can find a full guide to the API on the [reference pages](../../reference/index.qmd).

## Skim a dataframe and return the statistics

To use `skim()` in its default mode, see the quickstart on [the homepage](../../index.qmd).

If you want to export your results to a dictionary within Python, rather than printing them to console, use the `skim_get_data()` function instead. Let's see an example:

```{python}
import pandas as pd
from rich import print

from skimpy import generate_test_data, skim_get_data

df = generate_test_data()

summary = skim_get_data(df)
```

And the dictionary has contents as follows:

```{python}
print(summary)
```

The dictionary has one entry per section of the printed summary: `"Data Summary"`, `"Data Types"`, `"Categories"` (if there are any category columns), and then one entry for each kind of column that is present, such as `"number"` or `"date"`.

## What `skim` summarises

`skim()` groups columns by type and prints a separate table for each group. The statistics in each table are:

  | Section         | Column types                                                 | Statistics                                                                       |
  | ---             | ---                                                          | ---                                                                              |
  | number          | integers and floats                                          | NA, NA %, mean, sd, p0, p25, p50, p75, p100, hist                                |
  | category        | pandas `category`                                            | NA, NA %, ordered, unique                                                        |
  | bool            | booleans                                                     | true, true rate, hist                                                            |
  | datetime        | `datetime64` (timezone-aware values are made naive)          | NA, NA %, first, last, frequency\*                                               |
  | date            | Python `datetime.date` objects                               | NA, NA %, first, last, frequency\*                                               |
  | timedelta64[ns] | durations                                                    | NA, NA %, mean, median, max                                                      |
  | string          | strings (including object columns that contain only strings) | NA, NA %, shortest, longest, min, max, chars per row, words per row, total words |
  | All null        | columns where every value is missing                         | NA, NA %                                                                         |

\* `frequency` is the regular spacing of the dates that pandas infers (for example `ME` for month end), and only appears when there are more than three rows.

`NA` is the number of missing values and `NA %` is the percentage of the column that is missing. The `hist` column is a small unicode histogram of the values. For strings, `min` and `max` are the first and last values in alphabetical order, while `shortest` and `longest` are by number of characters.

Before summarising, **skimpy** infers a type for every column. You will usually get the best results if you set the datatypes you want yourself first (for example, `df["col"].astype("category")`).

### Columns that are left out

Columns whose values are a mix of types (for example, numbers and strings in the same column) can't be summarised, so `skim()` leaves them out of the summary. If *every* column is of a mixed type, you'll get a `ValueError` instead.

Dataframes with a multi-level column index (a `pandas.MultiIndex`) are not supported and raise a `NotImplementedError`. Flatten the columns first, for example with `df.columns = ["_".join(map(str, c)) for c in df.columns]`.

### Duplicate column names

If a dataframe has more than one column with the same name, **skimpy** gives the repeats a numbered suffix for the summary only, and tells you with a warning. Your dataframe is not changed.

```{python}
import warnings

dup_df = pd.DataFrame([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]], columns=["a", "a", "b"])

with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as caught:
    warnings.simplefilter("always")
    dup_summary = skim_get_data(dup_df)

print(caught[0].message)
print(list(dup_summary["number"]["mean"].keys()))
```

### Naming the summary

If your dataframe has a `name` attribute, it is used as the heading of the "Data Summary" table in place of "Dataframe":

```{python}
from skimpy import skim

named_df = generate_test_data()
named_df.name = "Test data"
skim(named_df)
```

## Clean up messy dataframe column names

**skimpy** also comes with a `clean_columns` function as a convenience (with thanks to the [**dataprep**](https://dataprep.ai/) package). This slugifies column names in **pandas** and **Polars** dataframes. For example,

```{python}
from skimpy import clean_columns

columns = [
    "bs lncs;n edbn ",
    "Nín hǎo. Wǒ shì zhōng guó rén",
    "___This is a test___",
    "ÜBER Über German Umlaut",
]
messy_df = pd.DataFrame(columns=columns, index=[0], data=[range(len(columns))])
print("Column names:")
print(list(messy_df.columns))
```

Now let's clean these---by default what we get back is in *snake case*:

```{python}
clean_df = clean_columns(messy_df)
print(list(clean_df.columns))
```

### Case styles

Choose a naming convention with the `case` argument. These are all of the options:

  | `case`              | Result        |
  | ------------------- | ------------- |
  | `"snake"` (default) | `column_name` |
  | `"kebab"`           | `column-name` |
  | `"camel"`           | `columnName`  |
  | `"pascal"`          | `ColumnName`  |
  | `"const"`           | `COLUMN_NAME` |
  | `"sentence"`        | `Column name` |
  | `"title"`           | `Column Name` |
  | `"lower"`           | `column name` |
  | `"upper"`           | `COLUMN NAME` |

For example, *camel case*:

```{python}
clean_df = clean_columns(messy_df, case="camel")
print(list(clean_df.columns))
```

The full set is also available in Python as `skimpy.CASE_STYLES`.

### Replacing text and keeping accents

Use `replace` to swap out parts of column names before they are cleaned. It takes a dictionary of `{old: new}` pairs. Matching ignores case, and each `old` value is treated as a [regular expression](https://docs.python.org/3/library/re.html), so escape characters such as `.` or `(` if you mean them literally.

```{python}
contacts = pd.DataFrame(columns=["FirstNom", "lastName", "Téléphone"])
print(list(clean_columns(contacts, case="camel", replace={"Nom": "Name"}).columns))
```

Accents are removed by default. To keep them, pass `remove_accents=False`:

```{python}
print(list(clean_columns(contacts, remove_accents=False).columns))
```

### Polars and duplicate names

`clean_columns` works the same way on **Polars** dataframes, and returns a **Polars** dataframe. If cleaning makes two names identical, the later ones get a number on the end, joined in the style of the chosen case:

```{python}
import polars as pl

pl_df = pl.DataFrame({"Total Sales": [1], "total-sales": [2], "TOTAL SALES": [3]})
print(clean_columns(pl_df).columns)
print(clean_columns(pl_df, case="camel").columns)
```

## Export the visual summary table to SVG

To export the figure containing the table of summary statistics, use the `skim_get_figure()` function. This will save an SVG file to the given (relative) path that you pass with the `save_path` argument. For example,

```{python}
from skimpy import generate_test_data, skim_get_figure

df = generate_test_data()

skim_get_figure(df, "summary_table.svg")
```

You can also specify other formats, such as HTML or text:

```{python}
skim_get_figure(df, "summary_table.html", format="html")
skim_get_figure(df, "summary_table.txt", format="text")
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: false

! rm summary_table.{html,svg,txt}
```

The function accepts both pandas and Polars DataFrames. It supports three output formats: SVG (default), HTML, and text. The function also prints the summary to the console; file paths are relative to the current working directory.

## Run skim on the command line

You don't need to be in a Python script or notebook to run **skimpy** on data! The package comes with a command line utility that can work with CSV, parquet, and SQLite files. When run on CSV files, it uses a powerful [duckdb](https://duckdb.org/2023/10/27/csv-sniffer) sniffer to guess column types.

You can run this with the below---but note that the command is `skimpy`, the name of the package, rather than `skim`, which is the command when used within a Python script or notebook.

```bash
$ skimpy file.csv
```

```bash
$ skimpy file.parquet
```

For SQLite databases, choose a table with `--table` (or its short form, `-t`):

```bash
$ skimpy file.sqlite --table <table name>
```

If you leave out `--table`, **skimpy** lists the tables in the database and then stops with an error asking you to choose one:

```bash
$ skimpy file.sqlite
Available tables in file.sqlite:
  - customers
  - orders
...
ValueError: Please specify a table using --table NAME or -t NAME (e.g., skimpy your_db.sqlite -t my_table)
```

To check which version you have installed, or to see the options, use:

```bash
$ skimpy --version
$ skimpy --help
```

## Settings

**skimpy** has a few module-level constants that control what goes into the summary. They are listed on the [reference pages](../../reference/index.qmd):

  | Constant                          | Default                   | What it controls                                              |
  | ---                               | ---                       | ---                                                           |
  | `QUANTILES`                       | `[0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1]` | The quantiles shown for number columns (as p0, p25, …)        |
  | `HIST_BINS`                       | `6`                       | The number of bins in each unicode histogram                  |
  | `MIN_COL_WIDTH`, `MAX_COL_WIDTH`  | `6`, `40`                 | The narrowest and widest a table column can be, in characters |
  | `MISSING_COL`, `COMPLETE_COL`     | `"NA"`, `"NA %"`          | Headings for the missing-value count and percentage           |
  | `NUM_COL_MEAN`                    | `"mean"`                  | Heading for the mean                                          |
  | `DATE_COL_FIRST`, `DATE_COL_LAST` | `"first"`, `"last"`       | Headings for the earliest and latest dates                    |
  | `NULL_VALUES`                     | `{nan, "", None}`         | Column names that `clean_columns` leaves untouched            |
  | `CASE_STYLES`                     | see above                 | The allowed values of `clean_columns(case=...)`               |

These are read each time you call a function, so you can change them for a session. For example, to use ten histogram bins:

```{python}
import skimpy

skimpy.HIST_BINS = 10
print(skim_get_data(generate_test_data())["number"]["hist"])
skimpy.HIST_BINS = 6  # put it back
```
